text.p: Iran's new president hailed the dawning of a new age in the Islamic republic, but the Shi'ite Moslem establishment of conservatives defeated in the election indicated the old one was not over yet.
Mohammad Khatami, a moderate former culture minister and middle-ranking clergyman voted into power by a landslide, said the country needed diversity of opinion to help achieve further development.
Elected on Friday, he is due to take over in August when President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani steps down after the maximum eight years in office allowed by law.

"Now the election has been completed...Islamic Iran has successfuly passed another test and a new era has begun in the shining history of the Islamic Republic," Khatami said in a statement quoted on Iranian state television on Sunday.
All forces, thoughts, opinions and skills were needed, he said, adding that the people should still pull together to resist threats from abroad.
But one of the right's main mouthpieces said the landslide was a vote for Islam and revolution rather than an individual.

Kayhan, the hardline Persian daily newspaper which speaks for the conservative establishment, said: "The 20 million votes Mr Khatami gathered were votes for the protection of Islam and revolution and no one can claim otherwise".
Earlier, Khatami called on Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei who gave him "appropriate guidelines", the official news agency IRNA reported.
The presidency is revolutionary Iran's highest elective office but ranks second behind the supreme leader, who determines policy and whose word cannot be challenged.
Iran's conservative Islamic establishment has been publicly licking its wounds following its performance at the polls, its worst electoral defeat in 18 years of revolution.
A majority of parliament, dominated by conservatives loyal to the main election loser, swung behind the winner with a public display of support.

Khatami's rout of conservatives through a mass turnout by a curious coalition of centrists, Islamist left-wingers, women, students, youths and intellectuals seeking change was Iran's biggest political upset since 1979, when fundamentalist Shi'ite Moslem clergymen led by the late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini toppled the pro-American Shah.
At the first session of the 270-seat assembly since it adjourned two weeks ago for the election campaign, more than 200 deputies pledged full cooperation with Khatami.
Nearly 200 deputies had supported Khatami's conservative rival, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, in the campaign while only 70 backed Khatami.
But Khatami won by a landslide -- 69 percent of a huge turnout of more than 29 million of Iran's 33 million electorate -- and trounced the speaker, who had to settle for 25 percent.
Nateq-Nouri said the massive turnout had surprised Western analysts and henceforth the Majlis would be an ally to Khatami and his government.
